screen.portable_pocket_cabin.fund_click: Click with items to deposit; click empty-handed to withdraw
screen.portable_pocket_cabin.fund_shift_: Shift-click this icon to fund from ordinary inventory stacks
screen.portable_pocket_cabin.install_boo: Consume one book to reveal the listed upgrades
screen.portable_pocket_cabin.book_empty: Place a cabin book in the slot to preview its upgrades.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.chopping: Cut into rough, even pieces with a knife. Pieces of the same size cook at the same rate, and smaller pieces cook faster and give more flavour to a dish.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.dicing.d: Cut into small, even cubes, so that every piece cooks through at the same time.
Cut into thin, flat pieces. Thin slices brown quickly in a hot pan and cook through before they dry out.
Cook meat or fish in a very hot pan. The heat browns the surface through the Maillard reaction, which makes much of the flavour of roasted food.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.frying.d: Cook in a pan with a little fat at a steady heat, so the inside cooks through while the outside turns golden.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.sauteing: Cook small pieces quickly in a little fat, moving them often. Mushrooms first release their water, then brown once it has boiled away.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.simmerin: Cook in liquid kept just below the boil. Gentle bubbles soften vegetables and draw their flavour into the broth without breaking them apart.
Cook meat and vegetables slowly in a little liquid. Long, gentle heat turns tough connective tissue into gelatin, which makes the meat tender.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.baking.d: Cook with dry heat all around, in a closed oven. Starches set, sugars brown, and steam and gas from eggs make doughs and batters rise.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.drying.d: Lay food out in moving air, or in the sun, until its water is gone. Without water, the moulds and bacteria that spoil food cannot grow, so dried food keeps.
book.portable_pocket_cabin.kitchen: Kitchen: a 5x5 room whose stations use central storage
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.whittlin: Carve a stick into thin, pointed skewers with a knife. Soaking wooden skewers stops them burning on the grill.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.skewerin: Thread meat and vegetables onto a skewer in small, even pieces, so they cook through together over the fire and are easy to turn.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.strainin: Pour a mixture through a fine mesh or cloth to separate the liquid from the solids. Stocks, juices, and cheeses are strained.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.grilling: Cook over open heat on a grate. Fat drips away and the surface chars, giving the smoky flavour of food cooked over a fire.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.stir_fry: Toss small pieces in a little oil in a very hot wok, keeping them moving. They cook in moments and stay crisp.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.deep_fry: Cook food submerged in hot oil. The surface dries and crisps at once, sealing in moisture. Oil breaks down a little with every batch.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.cooking_: Pour batter into round wells over medium heat. When the bottom has set, turn each ball a quarter at a time with a skewer, so the raw batter runs down and the ball closes into a sphere.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.pressing: Squeeze prepared fruit or seeds under a slowly tightened screw. The liquid runs into the bottle, and the dry solids stay behind in the press.
Rub against the fine edge of the blade until it falls apart into shreds. Grated carrot gives up its juice in the press, and grated roots and coconut give up their starch and milk.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.threshin: Beat the dried sunflower head against the board until the seeds come loose, then pick out the seeds from the chaff.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.toasting: Dry-roast seeds in a pan without oil until they smell nutty and darken. Toasting deepens their flavour, as for Styrian pumpkin seed oil.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.making_c: Simmer fruit gently with sugar and a little water until the fruit bursts and colours the syrup. Strained and bottled, it keeps, and a splash diluted with water makes a drink such as saftevand.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.reducing: Simmer a liquid slowly, uncovered, so its water steams away. Four bottles of apple juice cook down to one of thick, dark syrup.
item.portable_pocket_cabin.sunflower_oil: The everyday frying oil. Pour it into a cooking pot or wok to deep-fry or stir-fry.
item.portable_pocket_cabin.pumpkin_seed_: A dark, nutty finishing oil for dressings, as in Styria. It smokes at frying heat, so it does not go in the pot or wok.
item.portable_pocket_cabin.apple_juice.c: Fresh-pressed apple juice, æblemost in Denmark.
item.portable_pocket_cabin.sweet_berry_c: A concentrate. Diluted with water, a splash makes saftevand.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.grinding: Crush and rub a hard ingredient between stones until it breaks down into a powder or meal.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.evaporat: Boil seawater hard until most of the water steams off. The salt crystallises out as wet salt, and the bitter liquid left over is nigari.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.slow_dry: Let wet salt dry slowly in the shade. The slower the water leaves, the larger the crystals grow, giving coarse salt flakes.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.pounding: Strike and grind with the pestle against the mortar's rough bowl, crushing crystals or seeds by hand.
item.portable_pocket_cabin.coarse_salt.c: Wet salt dried slowly in the shade grows these large crystals. In the sun it dries quickly into fine salt.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.crushing: Crush stalks or fruit between rollers or stones so their juice runs out into the bottle.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.boiling_: Boil cane juice hard until its water is gone and only a thick, dark paste is left. Its molasses stays in, which gives brown sugar and panela their flavour.
Leave a hot mixture to cool and firm up undisturbed, as panela sets into hard blocks of cane sugar.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.dissolvi: Warm sugar in water, stirring, until no grains are left and the syrup runs clear.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.carameli: Heat sugar on its own until it melts and turns amber. The sugar breaks down into hundreds of new compounds, which is why caramel tastes richer and slightly bitter.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.skimming: Leave fresh milk to stand in a wide pan. Fat is lighter than water, so the cream rises to the top over a day, and you skim it off into bottles, leaving skimmed milk.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.churning: Beat cream hard and long. The fat globules break and clump together into butter, and the thin liquid left behind is buttermilk.
Press and fold an ingredient with the spoon so that salt or another addition spreads evenly through it.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.whisking: Beat quickly to fold air into cream or eggs, so they turn light and hold their shape.
Heat milk gently to blood warmth, the temperature at which cultures and rennet work best.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.culturin: Add a little of a live culture to warm milk or cream and leave it covered. The bacteria turn milk sugar into lactic acid, which thickens and sours it and keeps spoilage away.
item.portable_pocket_cabin.buttermilk.co: Live buttermilk can start your very first yogurt. After that, a spoonful of yogurt starts the next batch.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.fermenti: Leave food covered so wild yeasts and bacteria can feed on its sugars. They make gas, acid, or alcohol, which raise dough, sour it, and keep spoilage away.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.feeding_: Give a sourdough starter fresh flour and water. The culture grows into the new food, so after half a day there is twice as much: one to bake with and one to keep.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.kneading: Push, fold, and turn dough until it is smooth and stretchy. Kneading builds gluten, the web of wheat proteins that traps the gas the leaven makes.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.proofing: Let shaped dough rest in a basket while the leaven fills it with gas. Proofed dough rises in the oven instead of baking dense.
Divide dough and roll each piece tight so it holds its shape as it bakes.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.rubbing_: Rub cold butter into flour with your fingertips until it looks like breadcrumbs. Fat-coated flour forms little gluten, so the pastry bakes short and crumbly.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.chilling: Rest pastry somewhere cool. The butter firms again and the flour soaks up the water, so the pastry rolls without cracking and keeps its shape in the oven.
Line a dish with pastry, then add the filling and close or crimp the edge.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.mixing.d: Stir ingredients together until they are evenly combined, and no more, so the dough stays tender.
item.portable_pocket_cabin.sourdough_sta: Keep one starter back. Feeding it flour and water in the crock gives two: one to bake with and one to keep.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.steeping: Soak an ingredient in liquid until its flavour or active parts pass into it. Cardoon flowers steeped in salt water give a rennet still used for Iberian cheeses.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.curdling: Warm milk with rennet and leave it still. The rennet makes the milk proteins knit into a soft gel, which is cut to let the yellowish whey run out of the curds.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.pressing: Squeeze curds in a mould. A light press gives a soft fresh cheese; a long, hard press drives out the whey for a firm cheese that can age.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.draining: Let soured milk, cream, or curds hang in cloth over the strainer until the whey drips away and a thick, spreadable cheese is left.
Soak food in strong salt water. Salt draws water out and makes it hard for spoiling microbes to grow, and it seasons the food all the way through.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.ageing.d: Leave food to rest somewhere cool for days. Its own enzymes and friendly moulds slowly break down proteins and fats, deepening the flavour.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.ripening: Let a soft cheese rest on the shelf while a white mould rind grows over it and softens it from the outside in.
item.portable_pocket_cabin.vegetable_ren: Steeped from the flowers of wild cardoon, found in meadows and savannas. Calf rennet will later be a second source.
Leave cider open to the air. Acetic acid bacteria turn its alcohol into vinegar. A splash of live vinegar, the mother, starts the next batch much faster.
Cook food in water at a rolling boil until it is tender all the way through.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.pickling: Keep vegetables in vinegar with salt or sugar. The acid is too sour for spoiling microbes, so pickles keep for months.
Pack fish or meat in salt. Salt draws out water, and without water spoiling microbes cannot grow, which is how salt cod crossed oceans.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.curing.d: Rub salt, and sometimes sugar, into meat or fish and leave it to draw out moisture. Cured food keeps much longer and firms up before drying or smoking.
item.portable_pocket_cabin.cider_vinegar: The first vinegar comes from cider left open for five days. After that, a bottle of vinegar sours new cider in two.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.making_r: Melt butter, stir in the same weight of flour, and cook it gently. The fat coats the starch so it thickens a sauce smoothly instead of forming lumps.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.making_j: Boil fruit with plenty of sugar until it sets. Apple pomace adds pectin, the fruit fibre that makes jam gel, and the sugar keeps it from spoiling.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.making_c: Stir cream into hot caramel. It bubbles hard, then turns into a smooth, pourable sauce.
item.portable_pocket_cabin.sweet_berry_j: Apple pomace from the press supplies the pectin that sets the jam.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.seasonin: Finish a dish with the seasonings its tastes want. Put them in the seasoning slots: each wanted taste raises the dish's quality, and an unwanted or doubled taste lowers it.
taste.portable_pocket_cabin.salty.descri: Salt itself: rock salt, sea salt, and everything cured or brined with it. A little salt makes most dishes taste more of themselves.
taste.portable_pocket_cabin.sweet.descri: Sugar and fruit: cane sugar, honey, ripe berries, apples, and the syrups, jams, and cakes made from them.
taste.portable_pocket_cabin.sour.descrip: Acid: vinegar, cultured dairy such as buttermilk and yogurt, and fruit acids. Sourness lifts rich and sweet food.
taste.portable_pocket_cabin.bitter.descr: Nigari, toasted seeds, cocoa, and greens. A touch of bitterness balances sweetness; too much takes over.
taste.portable_pocket_cabin.umami.descri: The savoury taste of glutamate: aged cheese, dried kelp, mushrooms, cured fish, and browned meat. It makes food taste deep and satisfying.
item.portable_pocket_cabin.salt.cookbook: Put seasonings such as salt in a station's two seasoning slots. A dish that wants their taste comes out seasoned, or well balanced.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.cracking: Break grain into coarse pieces with the pestle instead of grinding it to flour. Cracked rye gives rugbrød its chewy texture.
Leave grain or beans in water until they swell and soften, ready to grind or cook.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.wet_grin: Grind soaked kernels into a smooth, wet paste. Corn ground this way gives starch or dough.
Strip the papery husk from an ear of corn and keep both: the kernels to cook and the husks to wrap tamales.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.burning_: Burn wood in the oven as the ingredient, not the fuel, until only fine white ash is left.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.leaching: Pour water slowly through wood ash. What drains out is lye, an alkaline solution for nixtamalizing corn and making pretzels.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.nixtamal: Simmer dried corn with lye or lime. The alkali loosens the hulls and unlocks the corn's nutrients, giving hominy for masa.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.griddlin: Cook flat dough on a hot, dry pan, turning it once, until it puffs and browns in spots.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.roasting: Cook in strong dry heat until the outside darkens. Roasting grain gives it deep, toasty, coffee-like flavour.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.sproutin: Keep dried beans damp and dark until they put out pale shoots.
Beat a soft dough hard with the spoon until it turns smooth and elastic.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.emulsify: Whisk oil into egg yolk a little at a time. The yolk holds tiny oil droplets apart, turning two liquids into one thick sauce.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.shreddin: Cut a vegetable into long, very thin strips.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.making_w: Leave grape must covered in the crock. Wild yeasts ferment its sugar into wine, which here is a cooking ingredient.
Simmer malt and hops in water, then strain. The malt gives sugar and colour, the hops bitterness.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.shallow_: Fry in a thin layer of hot fat, turning once, until crisp and golden on both sides.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.gratinat: Bake a dish under cheese or crumbs until the top melts and browns.
screen.portable_pocket_cabin.cookbook.gr: Grows on %s, in light %s or brighter, %s.
screen.portable_pocket_cabin.cookbook.sh: It needs a roof over it for its last stage.
garden.portable_pocket_cabin.cilantro: Ripe cilantro gives its leaves. Leave it one stage longer to flower and it gives coriander seed, which also plants it.
garden.portable_pocket_cabin.elder_bush: Pick elderflowers while it flowers, or leave them to ripen into elderberries.
garden.portable_pocket_cabin.plum_leaves: Plant the sapling. The leaves flower, then bear plums; pick them and the tree fruits again.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.settling: Wash grated potato in water and let it stand. The starch sinks to the bottom as a white paste, and the water is poured off.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.removing: Cut the crust away so only the soft crumb is left.
Tear soft bread into rough, airy flakes rather than fine crumbs.
Leave a dough covered so its gluten relaxes and it stretches thin without tearing.
Roll dough out thin and cut it into sheets, rounds, or strands.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.diluting: Stir a strong liquid into water to weaken it.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.laminati: Fold butter into dough, roll it out, and fold again, six times. The hundreds of thin layers puff apart in the oven.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.cooking_: Cook flour into boiling butter and water until it forms a smooth ball that leaves the pan clean.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.cutting_: Cut rounds and rings from rolled pastry and stack them into shells.
Dip shaped dough briefly in lye and scatter coarse salt over it. The lye gives pretzels their dark, glossy crust.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.stretchi: Knead curds in hot water until they turn smooth and stretch into long strands.
Wind long strands of stretched cheese into a ball.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.winnowin: Crack roasted cocoa beans and blow away the papery shells, leaving the nibs.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.temperin: Work melted chocolate while it cools and warms again, so it sets glossy and snaps cleanly.
Warm solid fat or chocolate gently until it turns liquid, without letting it burn.
Turn an ingredient gently through a light mixture so it keeps its air.
Let a hot mixture rest until it is cool enough to handle and has set.
Press dimples into the dough and fill them with the topping before baking.
item.minecraft.dried_kelp.cookbook_note: Dried kelp is kombu, the base of Japanese dashi.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.crumblin: Crush dried leaves between the stones into fine flakes.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.layering: Build a dessert in layers in a glass, so each spoonful has a little of everything.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.thickeni: Cook down, stirring, until thick enough to hold its shape.
Bring the parts of a dish together just before eating.
garden.portable_pocket_cabin.wasabi: Plant the root on gravel beside running water, as in a cold mountain stream.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.charring: Cook over fierce heat until the skin blackens in patches, for a smoky flavour.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.blending: Mash and mix ingredients together into a smooth or chunky sauce.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.frying_s: Cook a blended salsa briefly in a little hot fat, which deepens its colour and flavour.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.shelling: Crack and remove the hard shell or pod, keeping what is inside.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.pressing: Push a soaked pulp through the strainer so the paste passes and the seeds and fibres stay behind.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.tying.de: Tie herbs into a bundle with string, so they flavour a stew and come out whole.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.blanchin: Drop into boiling water for a moment. Blanched almonds slip out of their skins.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.browning: Cook butter until its milk solids turn golden and smell of hazelnuts.
Crush soft ingredients together with the spoon into a spread.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.softenin: Simmer a dried ingredient in water until it turns soft and gives up its flavour.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.sweeteni: Stir in sugar until it dissolves.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.infusing: Leave flowers or herbs in a liquid until their scent passes into it.
garden.portable_pocket_cabin.cumin: It grows wild at desert oases. Plant the seed on farmland or sand with water within four blocks.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.settling: Leave a pressed oil to stand until the cloudy water and fine paste sink, and the clear oil sits above them.
garden.portable_pocket_cabin.olive_leave: Olive leaves give green olives at their first fruit stage. Leave them one stage longer for black olives. Both press into olive oil.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.cutting_: Cut steamed sheets into long, thin strips.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.rolling_: Roll leaves under the palm to bruise and twist them, so their juices meet the air.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.drying_t: Dry rolled leaves in gentle heat until they are crisp and keep.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.witherin: Spread fresh leaves out until they go limp and lose some of their water.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.oxidisin: Leave bruised leaves to darken in the air, as for black tea.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.stone_gr: Grind slowly between stones into a very fine powder that doesn't heat.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.salt_cur: Pack in salt so it draws out the juice and preserves the fruit.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.sandwich: Lay a filling between two pieces.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.wrapping: Fold a soft dough around the filling and seal it.
garden.portable_pocket_cabin.tea_bush: Picking ripe tea gives tea leaves. If the bush ripens with a roof over it, it gives shaded tea leaves instead, for matcha.
garden.portable_pocket_cabin.rice: Plant the seedlings in a water source one block deep, over dirt, mud, or farmland.
garden.portable_pocket_cabin.glutinous_r: Plant the seedlings in a water source one block deep, over dirt, mud, or farmland.
garden.portable_pocket_cabin.water_chest: Plant it in a water source one block deep, over dirt, mud, or farmland.
garden.portable_pocket_cabin.cinnamon_lo: Use an axe on the trunk to strip cinnamon bark. The bark grows back.
garden.portable_pocket_cabin.oil_palm_le: Pick the fruit from the leaves. Use a glass bottle on the palm trunk to tap its sap once it has filled.
garden.portable_pocket_cabin.coconut_lea: It grows wild on beaches and can be planted on sand. Use a glass bottle on the palm trunk to tap its sap.
garden.portable_pocket_cabin.cardamom: Ripe cardamom gives its pods and more seeds.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.sweating: Wrap blanched pods and keep them warm so they darken and their flavour develops.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.washing_: Rinse grated roots in water through the strainer; the starch passes and settles, and the fibres stay behind.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.extrudin: Press a stiff dough through small holes straight into boiling water.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.grinding: Grind so a little grit and texture remain.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.cooking_: Simmer until much of the water has gone and the flavour concentrates.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.pureeing: Grind a cooked mixture until smooth.
Rub off the dry husk to free the seeds inside.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.baking_i: Bake set in a tray of hot water, so a custard cooks gently and stays smooth.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.rolling_: Roll pieces of dough between the palms into small balls.
Toss in a dry starch so a thin layer clings.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.hollowin: Cut a lid and scoop out the seeds, leaving a shell to fill.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.bruising: Crush with the back of the knife so the aroma is released.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.cooking_: Stir flour into boiling water until it forms a stiff paste.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.scalding: Pour very hot liquid over starch so it swells.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.cutting_: Cut rolled dough into circles with a cutter.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.steaming: Cook over boiling water in the pot, so the steam cooks the food without soaking it.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.skimming: Lift the thick cream that has risen on settled coconut milk off the thin milk below.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.searing_: Pass fresh leaves briefly over fierce heat so they wilt and stop browning, as for yerba mate.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.warming_: Heat a sauce slowly without letting it boil, so coconut milk stays smooth and doesn't split.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.brewing_: Steep tea strongly in hot water, longer than for drinking plain, so it stands up to milk, sugar, or lime.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.temperin: Whisk a hot liquid slowly into eggs so they warm without scrambling.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.spreadin: Spread a honey and almond topping over the risen dough before baking.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.shaping_: Press warm rice with wet, salted hands into a firm triangle that holds together.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.curdling: Stir nigari or lime juice into hot milk, so the proteins clump into curds at once without rennet.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.scalding: Dip a carcass in hot water, well below boiling, so feathers and bristles loosen at the roots and pull out cleanly.
message.portable_pocket_cabin.hook.no_bl: Blood can only be collected from a fresh carcass, before it is scalded.
message.portable_pocket_cabin.hook.needs: Scald this carcass in a cooking pot first, so the feathers or bristles come away.
message.portable_pocket_cabin.hook.skin_: Skin this carcass with a knife, or sneak to take it down.
message.portable_pocket_cabin.hook.scrap: Scrape this carcass with a knife, or sneak to take it down.
message.portable_pocket_cabin.butcher_bl: Skin or pluck this carcass on a hanging hook first.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.renderin: Melt solid fat slowly over low heat, so the clear fat runs out and the crisp bits left behind can be strained off.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.extracti: Simmer skin, feet, and trotters for hours, so their collagen dissolves and the liquid sets firm when cold.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.roasting: Roast a dressed bird in one piece, so the skin crisps while the meat stays moist.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.simmerin: Keep bones and vegetables just below a boil for hours. Gentle heat keeps the stock clear.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.boiling_: Boil bones hard for hours, so fat and gelatin emulsify into a milky, rich broth.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.dry_curi: Rub meat with salt and sugar and leave it to cure for days. The salt draws water out and keeps it.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.shreddin: Pull cooked meat apart into fine strands with two forks.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.cooking_: Cook over gentle heat for a long time, stirring now and then.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.crisping: Fry until the fat renders and the edges turn crisp.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.blind_ba: Bake a pastry shell empty first, so it stays crisp under a wet filling.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.braising: Cook seared meat slowly, half covered in liquid, until it falls apart.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.marinati: Leave meat in a seasoned, often sour liquid until the flavour reaches the middle.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.frying_p: Fry curry paste in the fat that rises from coconut milk until it smells rich and toasty.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.stuffing: Fill a hollow vegetable or piece of meat.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.whipping: Beat hard until light and full of air.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.confitin: Cook meat slowly, submerged in its own fat.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.garnishi: Add fresh toppings just before serving.
Cut thin slices off the outside of a roast.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.assembli: Put the parts of a dish together.
Press a pattern into the topping with a knife.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.crimping: Fold and press the edges of a pastry to seal it.
technique.portable_pocket_cabin.poaching: Cook gently in liquid that barely trembles, so meat stays tender and moist.
